The article raises critical questions about whether Hong Kong's expanded elevated networks have learned to engage the street more deliberately through stairs, ramps, and public rooms, or whether they continue hovering as a parallel world, examining what it now means to live and design within a metropolis increasingly organized by vertical levels.
articles.whyItMatters: Hong Kong's vertical public realm offers crucial lessons for high-density Asian cities (and Melbourne's CBD laneways) on how elevated networks can balance pedestrian connectivity with street-level vitality, climate protection, and genuine public access—not just privatized through-routes—particularly as cities worldwide grapple with climate adaptation and intensifying urban cores.

articles.title: Five simple zoning changes that any city can make to increase housing affordability
articles.summary: Planning attorney Donald Elliott, author of 'An Even Better Way to Zone,' argues that zoning reform need not be rocket science and proposes five practical changes to dramatically boost housing supply. First, allow medium-density housing in commercial zones—an opportunity created by COVID-19's legacy of vacant strip shopping centers along arterials. Second, permit housing on institutional properties like churches and schools. Third, allow small-scale multifamily infill on large single-family lots. Fourth, eliminate arbitrary residential density limits (maximum dwelling units per acre or minimum lot area per unit) that function as 'belt and suspenders' regulations alongside existing height and setback standards, perversely reducing housing affordability. Fifth, legalize microapartments and co-living arrangements. Elliott emphasizes these are mechanically simple amendments—just updating permitted-use tables in zone districts—but notes greater supply alone may not bring prices down, though no long-term affordability solution exists without significantly increased supply. Each reform targets regulatory constraints within local government control, offering a concrete roadmap for communities seeking housing solutions without wholesale zoning code rewrites.
articles.whyItMatters: This provides a pragmatic toolkit for practitioners navigating the housing crisis, translating abstract zoning-reform rhetoric into specific, actionable code amendments that can pass councils and survive legal challenge while addressing affordability through supply-side liberalization.

articles.title: How Cities Design Public Life in the Shade
articles.summary: As urban heat becomes an everyday condition rather than an exceptional event, ArchDaily explores how cities are treating shade as civic infrastructure requiring long-term governance, maintenance cycles, and embedded care. The piece examines diverse strategies: Singapore's freestanding metal canopies and covered walkways extending continuous shade networks between transit stops; Spanish cities alternating between seasonal fabric canopies strung along pedestrian corridors and freestanding plaza structures that create temporary urban rooms; and purpose-designed shade elements integrated into streetscapes and public squares. The article emphasizes that the design problem isn't simply knowing where shade exists but ensuring strategic distribution—placing shade where people walk, wait, gather, and linger with enough continuity to shape real behavior rather than isolated comfort pockets. Critically, adequacy depends on governance: permitting constraints, irrigation access, liability frameworks, street design standards, and maintenance protocols determine what gets built, how long it lasts, and whether it remains functional. A canopy without upkeep becomes a hazard; a tree without adequate soil volume becomes a failed promise. The piece positions shade infrastructure as requiring the same spatial thinking planners apply to transit networks or green corridors—hierarchy, rhythm, purpose, and systemic integration.
articles.whyItMatters: This shifts shade from amenity to essential urban infrastructure, equipping designers with spatial frameworks and governance models to integrate climate adaptation into the everyday public realm as extreme heat reshapes how cities function year-round.

articles.title: Azerbaijan Declares 2026 the 'Year of Urban Planning and Architecture' as Baku Prepares to Host WUF13
articles.summary: President Ilham Aliyev has signed an order declaring 2026 the 'Year of Urban Planning and Architecture' in Azerbaijan, establishing a national framework focused on urban planning policy, architectural culture, and sustainable development. The declaration aligns with Azerbaijan's preparations to host the 13th World Urban Forum (WUF13) in Baku from 17 to 22 May 2026, organized by UN-Habitat under the theme 'Housing the World: Safe and Resilient Cities and Communities.' The forum will address the global housing crisis affecting nearly 3 billion people worldwide experiencing housing inadequacy, examining housing as a foundation for inclusive, resilient, and sustainable urban development linked to integrated planning, climate adaptation, and inclusive governance. The organizers note the significance of 2026 as a milestone year, marking a decade since the adoption of the New Urban Agenda at Habitat III in Quito, coinciding with the UN Secretary-General's mid-term review and the assessment of SDG 11 at the High-Level Political Forum. Azerbaijan's Chairman of the State Committee on Urban Planning and Architecture, Anar Guliyev, has been coordinating with regional partners including Kyrgyzstan to build strategic partnerships and encourage participation in WUF13. The initiative positions Azerbaijan within global discussions on housing, sustainability, and the future of cities while emphasizing balanced regional development and alignment with international sustainability frameworks.
articles.whyItMatters: This signals a major international urban policy moment as the World Urban Forum provides a critical platform for global housing and urban development debates, with particular relevance for practitioners working on SDG implementation, climate-responsive planning, and housing adequacy frameworks at city scale.

articles.title: How Five Texas Convention Centres Are Changing the State's Biggest Cities
articles.summary: Nearly $9 billion in convention centre design and construction is currently underway across Texas's five biggest cities—Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Houston, and San Antonio—representing a significant shift in how these once-hermetic buildings that disrupted the urban environment are being reimagined to create connections through the city fabric. Michael Lockwood, senior principal at Populous overseeing projects in Dallas, Houston and San Antonio, attributes the resurgence to a 'perfect storm of conditions' driven by changing state legislation and a comeback for in-person business meetings. Modifications to state legislation have allowed municipalities to tap into additional funding for renovations, expansions and rebuilds. In Austin, the convention centre project—a joint venture by LMN Architects and Page—relocates loading docks and 336,000 square feet of exhibition space below ground to reconnect the urban grid of downtown, recreating the scale of city blocks and reducing the overall footprint. The project aims to become the first International Living Future Institute-certified carbon-neutral convention centre globally, with carbon reduction elements including heavy timber structure in the ballroom and reuse of materials from the demolished building. Fort Worth announced the second phase of its $700 million convention centre project in early February 2026. The trend reflects cities' desire to reduce 'dark days'—set up and tear down time—by hosting overlapping events in different portions of facilities, allowing for rolling rental income while integrating facilities more thoughtfully with their urban contexts.
articles.whyItMatters: The scale of investment and the shift from hermetic mega-structures to urban-integrated, carbon-conscious designs illustrates how cities are using policy levers and large public infrastructure to reconnect fragmented downtowns while addressing climate goals—a model applicable to convention districts globally.

articles.title: Milan Design Week 2026 Selection and Wasl Tower in Dubai: This Week's Review
articles.summary: This week's urban developments highlight how architecture continues to mediate between preservation and transformation through strategies of access and adaptive reuse across multiple scales and geographies. In Rome, STARTT's Pantheon Micro Architectures for Archaeology project introduces a new visitor route through previously inaccessible areas behind the Rotunda, revealing layers of archaeological fabric while maintaining clear distinction between contemporary interventions and ancient material—rather than restoring the monument itself, the project reframes its broader urban and historical context. A parallel approach emerges in Minneapolis, where Minoru Yamasaki's former Northwestern National Life Insurance Company headquarters is set to be converted into a hotel, demonstrating adaptive reuse of mid-century corporate architecture. Meanwhile, in Rome's Municipio XIII, Piazza della Stazione Cornelia has been transformed from a parking area and weekly market site into a structured public space with complementary green landscaped zones with newly planted trees and shaded resting areas alongside mineral paved surfaces designed for flexible use and community activities. A continuous paving strategy ties the composition together while the adjacent municipal building, now home to the Biblioteca Cornelia, extends the intervention's civic role with co-working, study, and multifunctional community spaces, reinforcing the square as a focal point of social and urban exchange. These developments reflect processes of transformation, reinterpretation, and public engagement that operate across multiple temporalities, balancing preservation with contemporary use and spatial continuity with evolving cultural programs.
articles.whyItMatters: The projects demonstrate how tactical urban interventions—from archaeological access strategies to parking-to-plaza conversions—can recalibrate existing urban fabric without wholesale redevelopment, offering replicable models for heritage-sensitive placemaking and incremental urban repair.

articles.title: SA and WA rank highest in 2026 planning reform scorecard
articles.summary: The Housing Institute of Australia has released its 2026 Planning Blueprint Scorecard, evaluating states and territories on planning system reforms against the federal government's 2023 National Planning Reform Blueprint. South Australia and Western Australia tied for top position with scores of three out of five, attributed to large-scale rezoning and land release programs, expanded development assessment panels in WA, and digital innovations including a land supply dashboard in SA. Victoria and the ACT tied second with 2.5 out of 5, followed by NSW and Tasmania at 2.0. NSW showed the most progress, advancing from 1.5 in 2025 due to pre-endorsed design pattern books and a new development coordination authority. Disappointingly, no jurisdiction scored higher than three out of five on planning reforms. The HIA called for Commonwealth leadership to provide a 'best practice' toolkit including AI-driven assessment software, supported by planning exemptions and digital portals. The Planning Institute of Australia warned the scorecard risks confusing reform intensity with actual planning system performance and quality outcomes, with CEO Matt Collins noting that 'communities don't experience reform' but rather whether homes get built, how long it takes, and whether infrastructure keeps pace. The HIA also flagged the absence of a federal government-led national dashboard tracking housing data on planning approvals, construction commencements, completion times and delivery constraints.
articles.whyItMatters: This systematic evaluation of state-level planning reform exposes the gap between policy rhetoric and implementation capacity across Australia, offering urban designers a framework to assess how regulatory change translates into tangible housing outcomes at the metropolitan scale.

articles.title: Can revolving loan funds revolutionize housing financing?
articles.summary: Benjamin Schneider's analysis for Remapping Debate examines the potential of revolving loan funds (RLFs) to unlock a new housing boom through a one-time public investment that cycles indefinitely. The concept originated with Montgomery County, Maryland in 2021, when the county created a revolving loan fund for housing production that policymakers now view as 'a simple, high-impact, and relatively cheap way to stimulate the development of new homes.' Unlike traditional grant programs, RLFs provide capital that is repaid and re-lent, creating a self-sustaining mechanism for housing production. Despite their appeal to many city leaders, the approach has faced political opposition from both ends of the spectrum. In progressive jurisdictions, housing advocates and politicians are wary of programs not directly focused on deeply affordable homes, preferring subsidies targeted at the lowest income brackets. Conversely, despite strong belief in market forces in other economic sectors, many Americans don't see a correlation between housing supply and housing costs, creating political resistance to supply-side interventions. The concept represents a middle ground between purely market-driven development and fully subsidized affordable housing, offering governments a way to leverage limited public funds more efficiently while supporting increased housing production across the affordability spectrum. Its success or failure may influence how municipalities approach housing finance in an era of constrained budgets.
articles.whyItMatters: Revolving loan funds present an innovative financing mechanism that could fundamentally reshape how cities deploy capital for housing, offering urban designers a scalable tool to unlock stalled projects while maintaining public accountability and long-term fiscal sustainability.

articles.title: New framework from Brown University evaluates urban design's impact on mental health
articles.summary: Researchers at Brown University have developed a groundbreaking framework to evaluate how urban design elements affect mental health disorders independently of pollution-related factors—representing the first methodology of its kind in the field. The framework marks a significant shift in how planners and designers can assess the psychological impacts of the built environment, moving beyond the traditional focus on air and noise pollution to examine design features such as street configuration, building scale, access to green space, and public realm quality. The new tool allows practitioners to isolate the mental health effects of urban form decisions from environmental contamination, enabling more precise interventions. While the research acknowledges the well-established links between urban density, environmental stressors and mental illness prevalence, the Brown team has created a systematic method for separating design-driven outcomes from pollution-driven ones. The framework is expected to inform evidence-based planning policy, development assessment processes, and urban design guidelines in cities worldwide. By quantifying the relationship between specific design interventions and mental health metrics including depression, anxiety, and cognitive functioning, the tool promises to elevate mental wellbeing as a core consideration alongside physical health, economic vitality, and environmental sustainability in urban planning decisions.
articles.whyItMatters: This framework gives urban designers an evidence base to advocate for design choices that support mental health—from street trees and human-scaled buildings to walkable neighborhoods—while demonstrating that good urbanism is not just about aesthetics or movement, but measurable public health outcomes.

articles.title: Apartment Sector Drags Down National Home Approvals
articles.summary: National dwelling approvals in Australia fell 10.5 percent in March 2026 to 17,300 homes, according to seasonally adjusted Australian Bureau of Statistics data released May 5. The decline was driven by a 26 percent drop in private homes excluding houses—primarily apartments—after February's 101.1 percent surge. However, private sector house approvals rose 0.9 percent to 10,194 homes, reaching the highest level since November 2021 and sitting 12 percent higher year-on-year. New South Wales recorded the largest rise in house approvals, up 9.5 percent to the highest level since August 2022, while Western Australia saw an 8.6 percent fall. Urban Taskforce Australia chief executive Tom Forrest noted that annualised results now touch 200,000 dwellings per year, still well below the National Housing Accord target of 240,000 completed homes annually. Master Builders Australia chief economist Shane Garrett warned that higher interest rates and escalating Middle East conflict pressures on construction costs will further constrain demand into 2027. The data underscores the challenge of delivering housing supply at scale: while house approvals are rebounding from subdued pandemic-era levels, medium- and high-density project feasibility remains constrained by elevated costs, tight contracting capacity and prolonged approval timeframes that squeeze margins through escalation and holding costs.
articles.whyItMatters: The divergence between strong detached-house approval growth and collapsing apartment approvals signals that Australia's Housing Accord targets will remain out of reach without policy interventions to make medium-density projects financially viable—a critical consideration for urban designers advocating transit-oriented and infill development.

articles.title: USDOT Proposes New TIFIA, RRIF Loan Sizing Methodology for TOD Projects
articles.source: The Transit Friendly Planning Newsletter (NJ TOD)
articles.summary: The US Department of Transportation proposed a new methodology on April 27, 2026 for sizing TIFIA and RRIF loans for transit-oriented development projects based on demonstrated transit value rather than traditional project finance metrics. According to a Nixon Peabody analysis, the approach would prioritize projects that measurably increase transit ridership and revenue through infrastructure improvements or revenue-generating joint developments such as ground leases or profit-sharing arrangements. This represents a significant policy shift: rather than evaluating TOD projects primarily on real estate feasibility, USDOT will now assess the degree to which a development enhances the performance and financial sustainability of the underlying transit system. The new framework aims to unlock federal loan capacity for mixed-use developments at station areas that have struggled to secure conventional financing due to the difficulty of underwriting the transit-adjacent premium. Projects demonstrating higher transit value—measured by factors such as increased farebox revenue, reduced operating subsidies, or improved network connectivity—would qualify for larger loan amounts and potentially more favorable terms. The proposal arrives as cities nationwide grapple with post-pandemic transit ridership recovery and seek to monetize publicly owned land near stations to cross-subsidize service improvements.
articles.whyItMatters: By directly linking federal financing to measurable transit system benefits, this policy recalibrates TOD incentives away from speculative real estate toward functionally integrated station-area development, offering urban designers a clearer mandate and financing path for projects that genuinely support ridership and network performance.

articles.title: Housing and conservation groups propose guardrails for housing on public lands
articles.source: KSUT Public Radio / Mountain West News Bureau
articles.summary: More than 60 conservation and affordable housing organisations have published "Shared Ground," a policy paper pushing back against proposals from members of Congress to sell federal public lands as a solution to the housing crisis. The paper, released on April 30, 2026, argues that housing affordability is "fundamentally a policy and investment challenge—not the result of a simple shortage of land." The groups include the National Housing Law Project, Nevada Housing Justice Alliance, Nevada Wildlife Federation, New Mexico Wild, Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, Conservation Colorado, Wyoming Wilderness Association and Wyoming Outdoor Council. Noëlle Porter, director of government affairs at the National Housing Law Project, noted affordable housing advocates were caught off guard when several congressional measures were introduced last summer, including proposals from Senator Mark Amodei (R-Nevada) and broader plans from other lawmakers. While those proposals failed, the groups wanted to establish criteria for any future plans. The paper lays out specific guardrails: legally binding affordability requirements, prioritising already-developed sites, excluding land with significant conservation, recreation or cultural value, and ensuring projects fit with local land use plans and involve consultation with Tribes and communities. The report acknowledges bipartisan interest in using federal land for housing—the Biden Administration launched a program to use Forest Service administrative parcels for employee housing—but argues that alternatives like preserving existing affordable housing, building on vacant land within existing neighbourhoods, and zoning reform should be prioritised. Meanwhile, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has his own plan announced over a year ago in partnership with HUD, but has made no public moves since, with HUD now the lead agency.
articles.whyItMatters: The paper offers a rare convergence of conservation and housing advocacy groups around a shared framework for evaluating public land proposals, signalling that land-use debates around the housing crisis are shifting from binary opposition to nuanced criteria focused on affordability guarantees, site selection, and community engagement—essential considerations for urban designers working on transit-adjacent or greenfield sites.

articles.title: Planning reform alone won't fix housing supply
articles.summary: The Planning Institute of Australia (PIA) has welcomed the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council's State of the Housing System 2026 report, released May 1, with PIA Chief Executive Officer Matt Collins noting that despite governments progressing planning reform, affordability continues to worsen and many approved homes are not being built. Collins said governments are taking significant action to improve planning systems and enable more housing, including streamlining approvals and supporting greater density, but feasibility and infrastructure issues mean too many approved homes are not progressing to construction, noting that "planning systems are getting better at approving homes, but feasibility and infrastructure issues mean too many approved homes aren't getting built." The report arrives as Australia pursues the National Housing Accord's target of 1.2 million new homes over five years, but delivery has fallen well short. The PIA response underscores a critical gap between planning policy reform—which state and territory governments have accelerated over 2024–25—and actual construction commencement. While planning bottlenecks are easing, the pipeline is now stalling at the feasibility stage due to construction costs, developer viability concerns, and infrastructure shortfalls. This positions planners as essential coordinators of a multi-sector solution that must integrate financing, building procurement, and long-term infrastructure sequencing to turn approvals into homes on the ground.
articles.whyItMatters: This highlights a structural disconnect that urban designers must navigate: regulatory reform enables supply on paper, but delivery depends on coordinating infrastructure, finance, and construction feasibility—domains often beyond planning's direct control but essential to housing outcomes.

articles.title: Hackensack Meridian Health Opens First-of-Its-Kind Wellness Center at NJ Transit Metropark Station
articles.summary: Hackensack Meridian Health's Health & Wellness Center at Metropark officially opened April 29, 2026, next to Metropark, New Jersey Transit's second-busiest train station, offering patients extended hours from 6 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. on weekdays to pop in for appointments before or after commuting. The $200 million center includes advanced imaging, urgent care, primary care, surgical specialties, medical specialties, retail pharmacy, physical therapy, occupational therapy, rehabilitation, and phlebotomy. The development is the first example of New Jersey Transit's broader LAND Plan (Leveraging Assets for Non-farebox Dollars), announced in October 2025, with NJ TRANSIT President & CEO Kris Kolluri describing it as "a model for what's possible under public private partnerships." The larger Metropark redevelopment by DOR—a consortium led by Russo Development awarded a $110 million tax credit—will add approximately 230 residential units with ground-floor retail. Hackensack Meridian Health is also consolidating its corporate headquarters into the building, uniting employees across several locations for the first time since the system's merger ten years ago. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill framed it as transit-oriented development that "makes it easier for residents to live, work, and access care without relying on a car, strengthening the connection between healthy communities and sustainable infrastructure."
articles.whyItMatters: This represents a new frontier for transit-oriented development: leveraging underutilized transit agency land for non-residential civic uses that anchor mixed-use precincts and generate non-farebox revenue, demonstrating how TOD principles extend beyond housing to support equitable access to essential services.

articles.title: Affordable Housing and Transit Series: New Jersey
articles.summary: New Jersey has emerged as a national model for integrating affordable housing mandates with transit-oriented development through a multi-layered strategy involving state agencies, transit authorities, and municipalities. The state's Transit Village Initiative—co-managed by NJ DOT and NJ Transit—has designated 37 transit villages as of 2026, providing priority funding, technical assistance, and grant eligibility to municipalities committed to redeveloping areas around transit stations. NJ Transit's policy requires 20 percent of newly built residential units in TOD projects on agency-owned land to be reserved for low- and moderate-income households. In October 2025, the agency launched the LAND Plan (Leveraging Assets for Non-farebox Dollars), a 30-year strategy to unlock the economic potential of its 8,000-acre real estate portfolio. If fully implemented, the plan projects up to $1.9 billion in potential revenue, 50,000 jobs, 20,000 housing units—including 4,000 affordable units—and $14 billion in state economic activity. NJ Transit plans to solicit development proposals for several sites in 2026 using a competitive public process. The agency has also partnered with Rutgers University's Voorhees Transportation Center to develop a Transit Friendly Data Application, which aggregates station-area data on demographics, land use, environmental conditions, real estate, and transit availability, giving planners and developers a unified resource to evaluate TOD potential across the state. Despite these tools, New Jersey faces a geographic affordability divide: the New York-Newark-Jersey City metro area scored 81 on the National Association of Realtors Affordability Index, placing it among the least affordable markets, while South Jersey shows relatively higher affordability ratios though renters still face significant challenges.
articles.whyItMatters: New Jersey's 30-year LAND Plan demonstrates how transit agencies can monetise underutilised land portfolios to deliver both infrastructure revenue and affordable housing at scale—a financing model relevant to Australian agencies managing large land banks near high-frequency transit. The 20 percent affordability requirement and integrated data platform offer templates for state-level TOD coordination that could inform upcoming reforms in Melbourne, Sydney, and Brisbane.

articles.title: Planning reform will make or break Australia's housing ambition
articles.summary: The Housing Industry Association has released its 2026 Planning Blueprint Scorecard, revealing that no Australian jurisdiction scores higher than three out of five in planning reform performance, even as the country falls 67,000 dwellings short of its annual National Housing Accord target. Under the NHA, governments committed to delivering 1.2 million new homes over five years to June 2029, but Australia must now deliver around 260,000 new homes per year nationally to meet that target—up from the original run rate of 280,000 due to accumulated shortfalls. New South Wales emerges as the most ambitious reformer, implementing state-led rezonings, expanded complying development pathways, pre-endorsed design pattern books, and creating a development coordination authority to tackle delays across the housing pipeline. Western Australia and South Australia record the highest overall planning scores for 2026, combining streamlined approval frameworks with consistent design codes and major land-release programs. South Australia's Housing Roadmap is supported by a modern digital planning system and land supply dashboard that demonstrates how cutting red tape and long-term supply planning can work together. Victoria is gaining momentum through deemed-to-comply standards for townhouses and low-rise housing, though these benefits risk being undermined by additional taxes and charges. Queensland records one of the lowest scores despite clear recommendations from the independent Queensland Productivity Commission. The HIA warns that restrictive zoning, outdated density controls, and excessive overlays continue to limit housing choice, particularly in well-located urban areas—in some capital cities, up to 80 percent of residential land remains locked into low-density zoning.
articles.whyItMatters: Planning reform is now understood as the system-defining constraint on housing delivery across Australia, determining not just approval speed but fundamental questions of land suitability, permitted yield, and design assessment—making it the critical battleground for addressing the national housing crisis.

articles.title: San Diego wants to limit upzoning law to just 16% of transit-adjacent parcels
articles.summary: San Diego is seeking delays and exemptions from California's new state housing law SB 79, which requires high-rise development near transit stops. The proposal would limit the law's application to just 16 percent of transit-adjacent parcels in the city. The city council is scheduled to take up the proposal on Thursday, May 8, 2026, and their decision would require approval by the state Department of Housing and Community Development. The story reflects broader tensions in California as municipalities grapple with state-mandated transit-oriented development requirements that override local zoning. The San Diego Union-Tribune reports that the city's approach represents one of the more aggressive attempts by a major California city to carve out exemptions from the statewide TOD mandate. The conflict highlights a recurring pattern where transit agencies and cities seek relief from housing laws despite the potential for increased ridership that comes from placing more housing near transit stations. The outcome could set a precedent for how other California cities negotiate with the state over implementation of TOD density mandates, particularly in jurisdictions where local political opposition to upzoning remains strong. SB 79 is part of California's broader strategy to address the housing crisis by concentrating new development near high-quality transit infrastructure.
articles.whyItMatters: The tension between state-mandated TOD and local implementation reveals how even progressive jurisdictions struggle to operationalise density near transit, offering lessons for Melbourne and other Australian cities now pursuing their own station-area upzoning reforms under state-led frameworks.

articles.title: Urban Trees Cool Cities More Than Expected, Not Enough
articles.summary: New research published two days ago reveals that urban trees reduce city heat more effectively than previously understood, but warns they cannot be the sole solution to rising urban temperatures. Cities and towns are typically 1–3°C hotter than surrounding countryside because asphalt, concrete, and brick absorb and radiate solar heat. While authorities around the world have promoted tree planting as a simple solution to urban heat islands, the research finds that current urban tree canopy cover typically addresses only a small fraction of excess heat. With ambitious planting programs, tree coverage could rise to around 20 percent of the heat mitigation needed, but a large majority of the extra heat will remain unaddressed. The study emphasises that trees must be seen as part of a broader urban design strategy rather than the whole answer. Clever urban design can reduce heat through reflective materials, increasing green spaces, and improving airflow between buildings. The research also highlights equity concerns: the people who need free cooling from trees the most are often the least likely to receive it, as lower-income neighborhoods typically have less tree cover than wealthier areas. Trees offer co-benefits including cleaner air and better mental health, making them valuable urban infrastructure even if their cooling effect is limited. The findings arrive as cities worldwide confront more frequent and intense heatwaves driven by climate change.
articles.whyItMatters: Urban designers must abandon tree planting as a singular heat-mitigation strategy and instead embed canopy within comprehensive urban form interventions—including materials, building setbacks, and wind corridors—that address the majority of urban heat island effects trees alone cannot solve.

articles.title: Belgian 'urban village' delivers social housing with style
articles.summary: Heulebrug, a 25-year urban development project in Knokke-Heist, Belgium, achieved 80 percent build-out with 851 living spaces combining market-rate, income-restricted, and publicly-owned social housing. Former mayor Leopold Lippens championed vernacular Flemish architecture, and the design team developed a 'simple yet precise one-page code of urban and architectural standards' governing roofs, windows, doors, and exterior walls. The development's northern and western edges integrate seamlessly with existing urban fabric, while southern and eastern edges face a greenbelt with a trail and right-of-way preserving views of open space described as a 'second coastline.' The first phase (2002) delivered 185 building plots, 26 social units, and 124 private apartments; the second phase (2017) allocated plots to young families with a 20-year resale ban to discourage speculation. The success has prompted more ambitious affordable housing policy for the entire city, with engineer-architect Mathias Delrue noting it demonstrates that municipally-sponsored development can transcend conventional 'housing project' perception.
articles.whyItMatters: This demonstrates that affordable housing and design excellence are not mutually exclusive—a vital lesson for Australian planners grappling with supply-affordability trade-offs. The one-page design code model offers a scalable, community-rooted alternative to prescriptive zoning.

articles.title: After Corbusier: How Southeast Asia Turned the Satellite City Into a Transit Megaproject
articles.summary: In Southeast Asia, modernist planning principles of rationalized, zoned, and infrastructural urbanism have been adapted under pressures of rapid urbanization, land scarcity, climate, and the need to house large populations quickly, resulting in a persistent 'apparatus' where modernism's afterlife is found not in the tower itself but in the city-making system enabling towers and supporting podiums, malls, and stations to proliferate. The 'satellite city' typology has been repeatedly retooled as new towns, mass housing districts, and more recently as transit-oriented development and rail-linked megaprojects. Transit-oriented development is widely adopted, but carries a risk: as station nodes intensify, urban life can become too concentrated, too internalized, and too controlled—reproducing superblocks and reducing the street's role as civic commons. The essay argues for reading Southeast Asian architectural history through the 'operating system' rather than icons—examining mechanisms that structure daily life at scale regarding where people live, how they move, where they gather, and what counts as 'public.'
articles.whyItMatters: This critical reframing of modernism's persistence in rapid-growth Asian cities offers crucial perspective for Australian planners designing TOD: the apparatus (density, mixed-use podiums, transit nodes) may be more influential than any single architectural gesture, but careful attention to public life and street networks prevents suburban repetition.

articles.title: What's on in May 2026
articles.summary: Melbourne Design Week returns 14–24 May for an 11-day program of talks, tours, exhibitions, launches, installations and workshops held across Melbourne. This year's program sees Japanese industrial designer Shunji Yamanaka delivering a keynote at the National Communication Museum, Alison Page presenting 25 years of practice at Melbourne School of Design foregrounding Blak design methodologies, and US architect Tom Kundig speaking on residential, commercial and cultural sectors. The 2026 MDW program celebrates Australian-made design by Danielle Brustman, Studio Shields, Dutoit, Thomas Maxam, Dean Norton and Tom Fereday, including an exhibition of the Design the World You Want International Student Ideas Competition at RMIT's Design Hub building and a conversation around naturalistic planting and restoring biodiversity to urban spaces. Beyond Melbourne Design Week, the heritage-listed White Bay Power Station in Sydney—recently restored and reconstructed by heritage architecture firm Design 5 and FDC Construction and Fitout—will open for tours between 18 April and 16 May as part of the broader Australian Heritage Festival celebrations. The programming reflects a strategic emphasis on design discourse, cultural heritage activation, and placemaking conversations that shape how Australian cities function as lived environments.
articles.whyItMatters: Major design festivals and public heritage activations are forums where urban designers engage with policy-makers and developers on liveability and adaptive reuse. Design Week's focus on sustainable placemaking, Indigenous methodologies, and international practice influence future precinct design and public realm thinking across Australian cities.

articles.title: Australia falling well behind national housing target
articles.summary: The housing accord has an ambitious target of 1.2 million new homes across Australia by June 2029. No state or territory is on track to meet its housing accord targets, with only 219,000 new homes built in the first five quarters of the agreement, well shy of the required run rate of 280,000 new homes, as revealed by the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council in its first quarterly report. The accord set an ambitious target of 1.2 million new homes across Australia over the five years to June 2029, but the national target is only on track to be completed by June 2030, with Victoria, Western Australia and the ACT the best performing jurisdictions, only set to complete their share of the target by September 2029. Measures such as relaxing zoning for middle density housing and removing third-party appeals for public housing appeared to be paying dividends for the ACT, with 117 per cent more dwellings approved in the year to January compared to the 12 months prior. The outlook for Victoria was less promising, with building approvals falling one per cent over the year to January, despite efforts to boost density in priority areas, streamlining approvals and a vacant land tax to unlock more space for development. The report underscores that planning reform, zoning reform, and density allowances are essential but insufficient on their own; state and territory governments must accelerate implementation and address systemic approval delays and infrastructure constraints.
articles.whyItMatters: For Australian urban designers and planners, this national tracking data reveals that zoning and density reforms announced across jurisdictions are not translating at the pace needed to address the housing crisis. The ACT's success with middle-density zoning and streamlined approvals for public housing provides a policy template, while Victoria's approval slowdown despite reforms signals that planning code change alone requires parallel investment in assessment capacity and infrastructure coordination.

articles.title: Missoula's Zoning Reform Raises the Bar for Small Cities
articles.summary: Missoula, Montana has completed a comprehensive zoning overhaul driven by the state's 2023 Montana Land Use and Planning Act (MLUPA), meeting the May 2026 deadline set by the legislation. The reforms mark a dramatic shift for the city, which had spent years resisting change—a 2012 ADU proposal passed only after contentious debate and produced just a handful of units due to attached restrictions. Under MLUPA, Montana's largest cities were required to relax zoning regulations to enable infill homebuilding and adopt faster project review processes. Missoula's new code now permits ADUs, garage conversions, apartment buildings, small-scale multiplexes, and townhomes by right on most blocks, with no density maximums. Mixed-use districts have no unit-count or floor-area-ratio caps, with height limits ranging from 4 to 12 stories. Nearly all residential neighborhoods now allow three-story buildings, with four stories permitted in central areas. Pushback emerged from the Rattlesnake neighborhood near downtown, where residents cited concerns about solar-panel shading and urban heat islands, prompting small zone adjustments. However, organized advocacy from groups like ProHousing Missoula ensured city leaders maintained the ambitious reforms. The overhaul is notable not just for its innovation but for its replicability, offering a template for similarly sized cities nationwide facing state-mandated housing reform.
articles.whyItMatters: This case demonstrates how state-level housing mandates can unlock locally stalled zoning reform, particularly in smaller cities where political inertia has historically blocked incremental change. The comprehensiveness of Missoula's reforms—eliminating density caps and enabling by-right development—offers a scalable model for jurisdictions grappling with affordability crises.

articles.title: Jersey City Approves 55-Story Tower With Whole Foods Market
articles.summary: The Jersey City Planning Board approved an 840-unit mixed-use residential tower in the Journal Square neighborhood on April 28, 2026, marking a significant transit-oriented development adjacent to the Journal Square Transportation Center. The 55-story project will include 84 affordable housing units and feature a ground-floor Whole Foods Market, with zero car parking spaces—a bold move that leverages the site's exceptional transit connectivity via NJ TRANSIT and PATH rail services. The development represents a new wave of car-free, high-density housing near major transit hubs in New Jersey, aligning with state and regional goals to concentrate residential growth around rail stations. Journal Square has been identified as a key growth node in Hudson County's planning framework, with the intersection of multiple transit lines making it one of the most accessible locations outside Manhattan. The approval follows New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill's recent executive order aimed at accelerating housing production across the state, including directives for NJ TRANSIT to identify underutilized agency-owned properties suitable for transit-oriented development. The project's mix of market-rate and affordable units, combined with its rejection of automobile parking, signals a planning approach that prioritizes walkability, transit ridership, and urban density over car accommodation—a strategy increasingly adopted by cities seeking to address housing shortages while reducing transportation emissions.
articles.whyItMatters: This project exemplifies the emerging generation of car-free TOD in North America, demonstrating how jurisdictions can leverage transit infrastructure to unlock dense, mixed-income housing while challenging automobile-centric development norms—a model Melbourne and other cities are actively exploring.

articles.title: Brisbane Reveals Density Shift to Unlock 6000 Homes
articles.summary: Brisbane City Council has proposed significant planning reforms targeting low-to-medium density residential (LMR) zones as part of its 'More Homes, Sooner' initiative, which could unlock approximately 6,000 new homes across 14 percent of Brisbane's residential areas. The reforms, announced following a May 2026 review by Mayor Adrian Schrinner, would increase allowable building heights from 2-3 storeys to a baseline of 3 storeys, with up to 4 storeys permitted near frequent public transport or retail centres. Minimum lot sizes would drop dramatically from 260 square metres to 120 square metres, making townhouses, row houses, units and small apartments more viable in suburbs including Morningside, St Lucia, Moorooka and Zillmere. The reforms also simplify development assessment processes and expand subdivision eligibility from 200 metres to 300 metres from shopping centres. The initiative responds to a sharp decline in LMR zone development, which has fallen from around 1,100 homes annually to just 445 in 2023 as rising construction costs have made smaller projects commercially challenging. City Planning chair Adam Allan noted that the reforms would empower private developers, who deliver 96 percent of Brisbane's homes, to respond to demand from more than 600 people moving to the city each week. The proposal follows similar density reforms in Sydney, where the NSW Government's Low and Mid-Rise Housing Policy opened low-density zones across metropolitan areas to dual occupancies, terraces, townhouses and small apartments within 800 metres of transit or town centres from February 2025.
articles.whyItMatters: Brisbane's reforms represent a critical shift from car-dependent sprawl to transit-oriented infill, demonstrating how mid-tier Australian cities are deploying policy levers—lot size reductions, height bonuses near transit, and streamlined approvals—to unlock missing-middle housing at scale in established suburbs.

articles.title: First Approval for 1625-Home Suburb in Sydney's South-West
articles.summary: Landcom, New South Wales' public development agency, has secured approval for the first stage of Macarthur Gardens North, a 1,625-home precinct in Sydney's south-west, marking a significant milestone in the state's affordable housing pipeline. The initial approval covers a 130-unit affordable housing building designed by DKO Architects, comprising 64 one-bedroom, 59 two-bedroom, and 7 three-bedroom apartments with a floor space ratio of 2.2:1 yielding 10,753 square metres of gross floor area. All 130 apartments are dedicated to affordable housing. The broader precinct represents one of several major projects Landcom is advancing to address housing supply, including redevelopment of tunnelling dive sites from the WestConnex and metro infrastructure projects. Recent milestones include a $236 million essential worker housing tower approved in Annandale in December 2025, which will kickstart a 580-home precinct, and a $152 million Chatswood dive site project exhibited in March 2026 that will eventually yield up to 1,500 homes for essential workers. Additional Landcom projects in development include a 3,900-home precinct at Glenfield, 15 kilometres from Campbelltown, and a 1,300-home district at Bella Vista, demonstrating the agency's strategic role in delivering affordable and workforce housing across Sydney's growth corridors.
articles.whyItMatters: Landcom's multi-site affordable housing pipeline illustrates how public land agencies are leveraging transit infrastructure sites and greenfield precincts to deliver scale, with dedicated affordable and essential-worker allocations becoming a standard planning outcome rather than an afterthought.

articles.title: Transit-oriented development projects continue to reshape American cities
articles.summary: A wave of transit-oriented development (TOD) projects totalling over $1.8 billion is reshaping American cities through mixed-use districts anchored by metro stations and transit hubs. In Washington, D.C., officials announced plans to transform underutilized Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority property surrounding the Takoma Metro station into a $200 million mixed-use community delivering 430-440 multifamily housing units—at least 15 percent designated as affordable—alongside 15,000-18,000 square feet of ground-floor retail connecting to the existing Takoma corridor. In Baltimore, Maryland is preparing a $1.5 billion redevelopment of the State Center site as a transit-oriented mixed-use district near the State Center Metro Subway station, Cultural Center Light Rail station, and within walking distance of Penn Station, making it one of the city's most transit-accessible development sites. Little Rock's Rock Region METRO is overseeing a $20 million project to transform the River Cities Travel Center into a mixed-use development featuring multifamily housing, retail, community spaces, health facilities, and administrative offices designed as a walkable district with improved pedestrian connections. In Honolulu, a $135 million project near Kūwili Station is part of a broader $1.6 billion infrastructure effort covering approximately 555 acres of the Iwilei-Kapālama corridor, with plans for over 1,000 affordable housing units supported by retail, community facilities, new streets connecting to the waterfront, multi-use paths, and bicycle facilities. Design and planning activities for most projects are expected to continue through 2026, with procurement solicitations anticipated in 2027.
articles.whyItMatters: These cross-country TOD investments demonstrate a convergence on mixed-use, mixed-income districts as the delivery mechanism for housing near transit, with federal funding driving cities to coordinate infrastructure, housing targets, and pedestrian realm design at the precinct scale rather than site-by-site.

articles.title: Adelaide Aquatic Centre by JPE Design Studio in collaboration with Warren and Mahoney and Karl Winda Telfer
articles.summary: Published May 5, 2026, this piece examines the newly completed Adelaide Aquatic Centre, which replaces an existing facility on the city's historic Park Lands—a 760-hectare green belt more than twice the size of New York's Central Park that has remained largely intact since Colonel William Light's 1837 colonial plan. The design team, led by JPE Design Studio with Warren and Mahoney and Cultural Creative Karl Winda Telfer, adopted what Telfer calls 'Country Aligned Design,' sitting on site to uncover sight lines and water stories. The cultural landscape approach softened the architecture's edges, introduced curves, and returned 1,000 square metres to the Park Lands. The broader site includes 15 hectares of landscape design, over 300 new trees, and water-sensitive urban design principles in the reinstated former car park. Height limits range from 3 to 4 stories in mixed-use zones nearby, with some reaching 10-12 stories. Building on Adelaide's Park Lands remains politically fraught; the commission is described as both a professional privilege and a social challenge, given the Park Lands' cultural significance as the city's lungs and urban moat. The mass timber interiors add warmth, while the scheme balances civic infrastructure with a commitment to landscape restoration and First Nations-led placemaking.
articles.whyItMatters: This project demonstrates how major civic infrastructure can navigate heritage constraints and deliver net-positive landscape outcomes through Country-led design methodologies, offering a replicable model for integrating Indigenous knowledge systems into contested public realm projects.

articles.title: Breaking the Single-Family Zoning Bottleneck
articles.summary: This May 3, 2026 analysis examines the nationwide movement to legalize 'Missing Middle Housing'—cottage courts, townhouses, and fourplexes that sit between single-family homes and high-rise apartments—as a strategy to address housing supply inelasticity. The piece outlines four key reform mechanisms now deployed across jurisdictions: ending single-family exclusivity by allowing duplexes and triplexes by-right without variance permits; fast-tracking Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) approvals to add rental income and supply; eliminating parking minimums and increasing density around transit hubs under Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) frameworks; and state-level overrides that mandate minimum density requirements to counter local NIMBY sentiment. The political debate pits opponents who cite property values, infrastructure strain, and neighborhood character against YIMBY proponents who argue the social cost of housing instability outweighs aesthetic uniformity. Economically, the article frames density reform as a question of supply elasticity: when housing supply cannot grow regardless of price, prices skyrocket. While reforms alone may not instantly lower prices due to construction costs and labor shortages, they prevent extreme price spikes from artificial scarcity and diversify housing types to serve broader income levels. The piece emphasizes that reforms are spreading from progressive cities to red states, including Georgia's tiny home bills and Georgia HB 1166, which allows secondary units under 400 square feet without local zoning approval.
articles.whyItMatters: Missing Middle legalization is emerging as the core battleground in North American housing policy, shifting from voluntary local action to state-mandated standards that preempt exclusionary zoning—a trend with direct relevance to Australian infill and medium-density debates.

articles.title: FTA Announces $28.5 Million for Transit-Oriented Development Planning
articles.summary: The U.S. Federal Transit Administration announced on May 11, 2026, that $28.5 million is now available through its Fiscal Year 2026 Pilot Program for Transit-Oriented Development Planning. The competitive grant program supports local communities seeking to integrate land use and transportation planning around new fixed-guideway or core-capacity transit capital investments. Applications are due by July 10, 2026. The program aims to enhance economic development, increase transit ridership, facilitate multimodal connectivity, and encourage private sector participation in TOD projects. Priority considerations for funding include safety—how projects create safe routes to schools, childcare, and social services along transit corridors—and innovation, including partnerships with transit agencies and advocates. The program represents a continuation of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act's emphasis on comprehensive planning that links housing, land use, and transportation. There is no minimum or maximum grant award amount, and projects may receive less than requested. The program explicitly encourages planning that supports affordable housing around transit, mixed-use development, and pedestrian and bicycle access to transit hubs. FTA noted the program helps fulfill its mission of building 'Great American Communities' by maintaining or expanding capacity for all travel modes while improving public well-being and climate resilience.
articles.whyItMatters: Federal TOD planning grants signal ongoing U.S. policy momentum toward integrating land use and transit investment, offering a model for coordinated intergovernmental funding that Australian practitioners can benchmark as states and territories grapple with similar coordination challenges around metro and light-rail projects.

articles.title: Trump's Transportation Secretary Announces $28.5 Million Investment to Make Mass Transit More Family Friendly
articles.summary: On May 11, 2026, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy announced a $28.5 million Notice of Funding Opportunity through the Federal Transit Administration's Pilot Program for Transit-Oriented Development Planning. The revamped program shifts federal TOD priorities toward safety, innovation, and family-centered design, with applications due July 10, 2026. The NOFO prioritizes three key criteria: safety improvements along transit corridors and at stations, particularly routes to schools, childcare, and recreation; innovative approaches and public-private partnerships to deliver TOD infrastructure; and increasing transit access for families, including integrating childcare and recreation near public transportation hubs. Secretary Duffy framed the initiative as part of President Trump's agenda to make commuting easier and more affordable for families, stating the program will invest in corridors that connect families to jobs, education, and healthcare. The funding represents a notable policy reorientation for the federal TOD program, which previously emphasized density, housing supply, and climate goals. The new priorities signal federal interest in leveraging transit planning for social infrastructure and family services, rather than solely housing production or emissions reduction.
articles.whyItMatters: This federal policy pivot toward family-oriented TOD introduces new evaluation criteria that urban designers and transit planners must now address—childcare proximity, recreation access, and safe routes for children—potentially reshaping station-area plans and TOD feasibility studies across the U.S.

articles.title: Above the Tracks: China's Unique Model for Transit-Oriented Development
articles.summary: Published May 8, 2026, Anderson Chider Hsieh examines China's distinctive approach to transit-oriented development, where cities since 2010 have increasingly built mixed-use neighborhoods directly above metro depots and rail yards. The model leverages large tracts of state-owned land near transit infrastructure to create dense, integrated communities atop operational rail facilities. Hsieh's analysis, drawing on examples from Shenzhen and other Chinese cities, highlights how this vertical integration maximizes land value and transit access while maintaining depot functionality below. The approach contrasts sharply with Western TOD models, which typically redevelop adjacent parcels but leave depot sites untouched due to fragmented land ownership, operational constraints, and regulatory barriers. Hsieh argues that U.S. transit agencies could reevaluate the redevelopment potential of their extensive rail yards and depot holdings, which often occupy prime, transit-accessible land in inner-city locations. The article suggests that air-rights development and deck-over strategies could unlock significant housing and mixed-use capacity, though institutional barriers—including federal restrictions on non-transit revenue generation and local zoning—would need reform. The piece positions depot-top development as an untapped frontier for North American TOD, particularly as housing crises intensify pressure to maximize land near existing infrastructure.
articles.whyItMatters: China's depot-top urbanism offers a provocative model for Western cities facing acute land scarcity near transit—challenging planners to rethink rail yards not as off-limits operational zones but as development platforms that could yield thousands of homes on publicly owned, transit-rich sites.

articles.title: The Australian Housing Landscape as of March 2026
articles.summary: BDO's inaugural housing market pulse, published in late April 2026, provides a state-by-state analysis of Australia's housing sector as of March 2026, examining policy reforms, market conditions, and delivery challenges. New South Wales emerges as the most ambitious reformer, with state-led rezonings, expanded complying development pathways, pre-endorsed design pattern books, and the creation of a development coordination authority all signaling serious attempts to tackle pipeline delays. The reforms emphasize higher-density supply in established locations and around transport corridors, with faster approvals and streamlined development pathways designed to support infill housing. However, BDO notes that feasibility remains challenging due to elevated construction costs, tight contracting capacity, and prolonged approval and mobilization timeframes, which squeeze margins through escalation and holding costs. Victoria entered 2026 with subdued conditions as buyers remain price-sensitive and activity concentrates in more affordable segments. Queensland remained one of Australia's best-performing markets in 2025, with Brisbane house prices increasing approximately 9 percent over the year and regional markets recording 13-14 percent growth driven by lifestyle demand and interstate migration, though signs of moderation emerged in late 2025 as affordability tightened. Unit rents stabilized in late 2025, suggesting affordability pressures may be tempering demand. The report emphasizes that long-term delivery will require sustained collaboration, infrastructure investment, and ongoing policy refinement, with stronger tenancy laws expected to enhance renter stability though investor sentiment may remain cautious.
articles.whyItMatters: NSW's comprehensive planning reforms—combining rezoning, pattern books, and a new delivery authority—represent Australia's most assertive institutional response to housing undersupply, offering a potential blueprint (or cautionary tale) for other states grappling with the National Housing Accord's 1.2 million dwelling target.

articles.title: AUO Launches 24 New Housing Indicators for Inclusive Urban Planning
articles.summary: The Australian Urban Observatory (AUO), in partnership with RMIT's Centre for Urban Research, has released 24 new mapped housing indicators covering Australia's 21 largest cities, providing granular data at neighbourhood, suburb, and local government area levels. The publicly available indicators examine housing precarity, combined housing and transport costs, rental and mortgage stress levels, access to homelessness services, and key worker populations. AUO Director and RMIT Associate Professor Melanie Davern emphasised the indicators were co-designed with policymakers, service providers, and community advocates to understand area-based differences and shape effective policies. Nithya Solomon, Director of RMIT's Innovation Catalyst, highlighted that making this essential data accessible to everyone free of cost is crucial for inclusive cities and neighbourhoods. The AUO now features 48 indicators across nine domains covering liveability, walkability, social infrastructure, transport, and food and alcohol access. The initiative is part of RMIT University's social innovation and urban renewal programs, supported by the Victorian Government's Higher Education State Investment Fund.
articles.whyItMatters: This open-access dataset arms planners, councils, and advocacy groups with evidence to identify housing stress hotspots, calibrate affordable-housing targets, and test whether new TOD or infill proposals improve or worsen spatial inequality across metropolitan Australia.

articles.title: FTA Announces $28.5 Million for Transit-Oriented Development Planning
articles.summary: On May 11, 2026, the Federal Transit Administration announced approximately $28.5 million in available funding for the Fiscal Year 2026 Pilot Program for Transit-Oriented Development Planning. Applications are due by July 10, 2026. The program aims to help communities integrate land use and transportation planning around new transit projects, creating compact, mixed-use communities near transit where residents can easily access jobs and services. The initiative represents a federal commitment to dense, walkable, mixed-use development near transit, which officials say attracts people and adds to vibrant, connected communities. Public transportation can help foster partnerships that support the development of affordable housing around transit, according to the agency. Recent changes in federal law now allow transit agencies to repurpose qualified properties for development purposes. The funding continues the federal government's investment in transit-oriented development, which puts public transit in reach for more people and aims to improve quality of life in urban areas across the country. Transit-oriented development is defined as creating environments where housing, businesses, entertainment venues, parks, retail, restaurants, improved pedestrian infrastructure, and diverse housing choices are all accessible from transit stops.
articles.whyItMatters: This federal funding represents a significant policy tool for advancing transit-oriented development nationwide, providing planners with resources to integrate housing, land use, and transportation planning at critical transit nodes.

articles.title: Bay Area MTC Adopts $45 Million TOC Incentive Program with Extended Deadline
articles.summary: On February 25, 2026, the San Francisco Bay Area's Metropolitan Transportation Commission adopted a $45 million Transit-Oriented Communities Incentive Program as part of the One Bay Area Grant 4 (OBAG 4) funding cycle. On May 6, 2026, MTC staff hosted a webinar providing jurisdictions with an overview of the program and key updates. The program features a significant policy shift: the deadline for local jurisdictions to meet TOC standards has been extended to July 1, 2027, and credit will no longer be provided for work-in-progress given the fully incentive-based structure and extended timeline. All TOC areas subject to Senate Bill 79 will receive full credit for the Maximum Allowable Residential Density standard. The policy applies to locations within a half-mile of existing and planned stops and stations served by BART, Caltrain, SMART, Capitol Corridor, and ACE. Key program features include requirements for affordable housing production, preservation and protection, stabilizing businesses to prevent displacement, and improving transit station access. Jurisdictions can receive credit for one TOC housing protection policy through countywide programs or local policy, but credit for a second policy must be based on local implementation. Notably, jurisdictions may not receive credit for Protection Policy 2 (No Net Loss and Right of Return) due to recent changes in state law.
articles.whyItMatters: This regional incentive program demonstrates how metropolitan planning organizations can use funding mechanisms to drive local jurisdictions toward transit-supportive land use policies, particularly around affordable housing and anti-displacement measures—a model relevant for other metropolitan regions globally.

articles.title: FTA announces $28.5 million in funding for Transit-Oriented Development Planning
articles.summary: The Federal Transit Administration (FTA) announces the opportunity to apply for $28,492,618 in competitive grants for the Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 Pilot Program for Transit-Oriented Development Planning (TOD Pilot Program). As required by Federal public transportation law, Section 20005(b) of the Moving Ahead for Progress in the 21st Century Act (MAP–21), as amended by section 30009 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, and subject to funding availability, funds will be awarded competitively to support comprehensive or site-specific planning associated with new fixed guideway and core capacity improvement transit projects. USDOT says it is looking to partner with communities with proposals that advance safety, innovation and make commuting easier. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stated the revamped program will invest in transit corridors that connect families to jobs, education and healthcare, which can improve regional mobility. Evaluation criteria include innovation—how a project fosters innovative approaches, partnerships with transit agencies and advocates and promotes research, innovation and demonstration of new technologies and policies that stimulate private sector participation—and benefits for families and communities, including how a project increases transit access for families at the proposed transit station or along the corridor and how it integrates childcare and recreation near public transportation hubs. Project proposals must be submitted electronically through Grants.gov by 11:59 p.m. Eastern time on July 10, 2026.
articles.whyItMatters: The program signals renewed federal commitment to land-use/transport integration in the U.S., with a notable emphasis on family amenities and innovation—criteria that could reshape how planners pitch TOD projects and what gets built around stations.

articles.title: How cities are turning urban complexity into coherent climate plans
articles.summary: Cities are crucial to the climate transition – their buildings, energy systems, transportation and urban design offer interconnected opportunities to decarbonize. To secure investment in climate-related projects, cities must establish a vision, deploy systems thinking and collaborate across public and private sectors. Green City Action Plans, delivered as part of EBRD Green Cities, offer a framework for connecting environmental challenges with sustainable infrastructure investments and policy measures. Once identified, these projects need to be prepared for investment. If a city is targeting investment from a multilateral development bank (MDB), this requires a feasibility study and concept design. Does the new fleet of electric buses or the wastewater treatment plant make sense? What should the technical specifications be? To ensure a project is bankable, financiers must be involved from the outset. Infrastructure requires sizable investments, and it takes time to build trust. If MDBs are to invest, they will need to ensure that, right from the feasibility stage, a project meets their requirements. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)'s Green Cities programme fosters this kind of collaborative, long-term relationship with over 50 cities. The Green Cities programme identifies, prioritizes and connects cities' environmental challenges with sustainable infrastructure investments and policy measures. The article emphasises that climate action in cities is not simply a technical challenge but requires aligning vision, systems thinking, and cross-sector collaboration to make projects bankable and implementable at scale.
articles.whyItMatters: This operationalises the 'climate adaptation masterplan' conversation by showing how cities can move from aspiration to bankable infrastructure projects, a gap many municipalities struggle to bridge when translating urban design ambitions into funded works.

articles.title: Kerstin Thompson Architects and Nelson and Koo unveil design for 3.6-hectare Adelaide complex
articles.summary: Melbourne-based Kerstin Thompson Architects (KTA) and Nelson and Koo have unveiled designs for a $250 million mixed-use development in Forestville, Adelaide's inner south-west, on a 3.6-hectare former industrial site. Developed in collaboration with Commercial Retail Group and Renewal SA, the project involves a multidisciplinary team including RN Architecture, Studio Gram, Designinc, Matter Engineering, Lucid Consulting, Future Urban and Ellara. The architectural massing consists of three distinct forms: a mid-rise short-stay accommodation building fronting Anzac Highway, two apartment buildings in the centre, and a collection of terraces along the eastern boundary, unified by consistent materiality and datum lines. The scheme is anchored in principles drawn from global 'blue zones'—geographic regions identified by researchers as places of human longevity and wellbeing—embedding opportunities for social connection and walkability. At its centre, the development includes a market hall 'agora' and two external public realms conceived as 'plateia' (Greek communal meeting places). The sustainability-focused program includes an 'urban green school' and a 3,600-square-metre productive rooftop farm. Construction is anticipated to begin in late 2026, positioning the project as what KTA describes as 'a catalyst for urban regeneration' that supports daily life through thoughtful design and diverse community amenities.
articles.whyItMatters: This project demonstrates how large-scale adaptive reuse of former industrial sites can integrate mixed-use density with blue zone wellbeing principles, productive urban agriculture, and public realm innovation—offering a replicable model for inner-urban regeneration in Australian cities.

articles.title: Commonwealth Bank Downgrades Housing Price Forecasts Following Federal Budget Tax Changes
articles.summary: Commonwealth Bank has revised its national dwelling price growth forecast to 3 percent for the year ending December 2026, down from a previous projection of 5 percent, following the Federal Government's May 2026 Budget announcement of sweeping changes to residential property investment taxation. The Budget package centers on two major reforms: limiting negative gearing for residential property to new builds only, and replacing the 50 percent capital gains tax discount with cost base indexation and a 30 percent minimum tax rate. CBA economists estimate these changes will reduce house prices by approximately 3 percent below what they otherwise would have been, with smaller impacts on rents. The analysis suggests the removal of negative gearing is equivalent to a 90-155 basis point increase in investor mortgage rates in immediate cash-flow terms for highly leveraged investors with high marginal tax rates and low rental yields. However, the Budget design allows quarantined losses to be carried forward against future residential rental income or capital gains. The bank notes that three cash rate hikes earlier in 2026, taking the rate to 3.85 percent, have already subtracted 1.5 percentage points from price growth forecasts, and the ongoing Middle East conflict has increased construction costs and created supply uncertainty. The Budget also includes a $2 billion Local Infrastructure Fund, extended bans on foreign purchases of established dwellings, and strengthened affordability requirements for build-to-rent tax concessions.
articles.whyItMatters: This analysis quantifies how federal tax policy shifts directly impact housing affordability and investment viability, giving urban designers hard data on the interplay between fiscal settings, construction finance, and dwelling supply trajectories—critical inputs for feasibility modeling and precinct planning.

articles.title: To Improve Transit Service, We Need Better Transit-Oriented Development: The Case for Build HUBS
articles.summary: Transportation For America published an analysis on May 13, 2026, arguing that maximizing existing transit investments requires far more transit-oriented development to boost ridership and financial sustainability. The article highlights how low ridership traps transit systems in a "horrid cycle" where reduced fare revenue leads to service cuts, further undermining reliability. The proposed Build Housing Unlock Benefits and Services (Build HUBS) Act targets reforms to the Railroad Rehabilitation and Financing (RRIF) and Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act (TIFIA) programs to better support TOD and housing near transit. The piece cites Chicago's 2013 Wicker Park development—a 11-story building with 99 mixed-income apartments, office space, and ground-floor retail across from the Division Blue Line station—as a catalyst for broader neighborhood transformation and economic growth. It also profiles Hennepin County, Minnesota's 2015 light rail TOD project at Lake Street station, which delivered 500 housing units, retail space, and a Human Services Center, significantly improving access to services for residents. The former Metro Transit General Manager is quoted emphasizing that "transit-oriented development is about letting people choose where to live, work and recreate—and giving them the freedom to make those choices without worrying about the financial burdens they'll face when it comes to transportation." The article underscores that TOD strategies—building commercial and residential spaces in walkable proximity to high-quality transit—are essential to breaking the low-ridership feedback loop.
articles.whyItMatters: The piece connects transit viability directly to land use intensity, making the case that station-area densification isn't cosmetic but existential for service frequency and network resilience—a strategic rationale Melbourne designers can deploy when advocating for higher FSRs and mixed-use zoning around metro stations.

articles.title: Federal Budget 2026 ties housing tax reforms to $2 billion infrastructure fund for planning reform
articles.summary: Australia's 2026–27 Federal Budget introduced sweeping changes to housing policy, pairing contentious tax reforms with a $2 billion Local Infrastructure Fund designed to incentivise state planning reform. From 1 July 2027, negative gearing concessions will be limited to newly built homes only, while the capital gains tax discount will shift from a flat 50 per cent to an inflation-indexed model, though newly built residential properties may retain preferential treatment. Existing negatively geared investments are grandfathered, but CGT changes apply to all gains realised from 2027 onward. Treasury estimates the tax changes will reduce construction by 35,000 homes over the next decade, but the government argues the $2 billion infrastructure fund—which pays states to loosen restrictive planning laws and boost construction productivity—will more than offset this. Grattan Institute analysis suggests planning reforms could unlock more than 60,000 additional homes annually if states embrace well-located upzoning. CommBank economists forecast dwelling price growth will slow to 3 per cent in 2026 (down from an earlier 5 per cent estimate), driven primarily by three cash rate hikes this year rather than the policy changes themselves. The Budget also includes $45 million for single-touch federal-state approvals and commits to identifying surplus Commonwealth land—including 67 military sites—for housing. The measures are part of the National Housing Accord's 1.2 million homes target, which the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council now projects will be met in June 2030, one year late.
